home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Laval: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in Laval: 3 licensed organizations, local prices, Quebec rebates and what 67% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 3 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Laval. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Laval houses, and which Quebec rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Laval homes
sections.html:
Of Laval's 101,460 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 17% were built before 1961 and 67% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Laval house dates from 1971–1980, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Laval gets about 4,167 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −23.1°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Montréal International. That's about 6% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Montréal area, 54% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, 15% with a heat pump, 10% with a forced-air furnace and 6% with a boiler and radiators; electricity is the main heating energy for 71% of households, natural gas for 5% and oil for about 2% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

In Quebec, EnerGuide evaluations are booked through the provincial Rénoclimat program: the pre-retrofit evaluation costs $150 plus taxes, reimbursed when you receive financial assistance under the program, and the first post-retrofit evaluation is free.

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in Laval
sections.html:
Laval gets about 4,167 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −23.1°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Montréal International. That's about 6% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover.

Of Laval's 101,460 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 17% were built before 1961 and 67% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

• Combustion safety. In the Montréal area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 5% and oil for about 2% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in Laval
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. Health Canada's 2012 survey found 12.1% of 107 homes tested in the Région de Laval health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 17.4% (1 in 6) of houses at or above the guideline for Montréal Metro Area (Montréal CMA). Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. Radon testing in Laval

A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. In Quebec, EnerGuide evaluations are booked through the provincial Rénoclimat program: the pre-retrofit evaluation costs $150 plus taxes, reimbursed when you receive financial assistance under the program, and the first post-retrofit evaluation is free.

• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Laval: sizing a heat pump for −23.1°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Laval homes, sized to the local −23.1°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −23.1°C for Laval, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Montréal International.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Laval
sections.html:
−23.1°C is the 26th-coldest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −23.1°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Montréal area, 54% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, 15% with a heat pump, 10% with a forced-air furnace and 6% with a boiler and radiators; electricity is the main heating energy for 71% of households, natural gas for 5% and oil for about 2% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

sections.h2: Why Laval homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Laval gets about 4,167 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −23.1°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Montréal International. On Laval's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Laval's 101,460 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 17% were built before 1961 and 67% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (20% of Laval's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Laval: local levels, test kits and certified professionals
radon-testing.description: Radon in Laval: Health Canada survey results for the Région de Laval region (12.1% above the guideline), how to test for 3+ months, where to get kits and C-NRPP professionals locally.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 12.1% of homes tested in the Région de Laval health region were above the guideline, and the only way to know about your house is to test it.

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 12.1% of 107 homes tested in the Région de Laval health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 17.4% (1 in 6) of houses at or above the guideline for Montréal Metro Area (Montréal CMA).

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.
  • Place the detector in the lowest level you spend four or more hours a day in, away from drafts, and follow the kit's instructions.
  • If the result is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada recommends fixing it within a year, sooner if it's much higher.

Our full radon testing guide.

• The Association pulmonaire du Québec sells long-term detectors for about $50 including analysis, and some municipal libraries lend electronic monitors.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Laval postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

• Quebec's construction code requires a soil-gas barrier in new dwellings and, since April 17, 2025, a passive radon exhaust stack.
  • The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.
  • If your level is high, mitigation (usually a sub-slab depressurization fan system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional) typically costs $2,000–$4,000.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Laval?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 12.1% of 107 homes tested in the Région de Laval health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 17.4% (1 in 6) of houses at or above the guideline for Montréal Metro Area (Montréal CMA). Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with most of it during the heating season. Short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Laval?
faq.a: The Association pulmonaire du Québec sells long-term detectors for about $50 including analysis, and some municipal libraries lend electronic monitors. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits for about $30–$60.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Typically $2,000–$4,000 for a sub-slab depressurization system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional.

mold-testing.lede: Mold sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mold problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in Laval homes
sections.html:
Laval gets about 4,167 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −23.1°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Montréal International. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mold usually starts in Laval houses.

Of Laval's 101,460 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 17% were built before 1961 and 67% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

Quebec has a voluntary standard for handling mould in homes (BNQ 3009-600, 2020); no province has a mandatory residential mould standard.

Ask any Laval tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Laval · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mold testing cost in Laval?
faq.a: Plan on about $300–$600 for a typical sampling visit (a September 2026 planning range); lab fees for extra samples add to that.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Laval houses
sections.html:
Of Laval's 101,460 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 17% were built before 1961 and 67% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

In Quebec, CNESST rules require contractors to check for asbestos before any work that could release dust, and the province tells homeowners to have suspect materials checked by a qualified contractor or an IRSST-recognized lab and never to do asbestos work themselves. Quebec treats material as asbestos-containing from 0.1% asbestos, a stricter line than most provinces.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program or recognized by the IRSST in Quebec.

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in Laval?

In Quebec, CNESST rules require contractors to check for asbestos before any work that could release dust, and the province tells homeowners to have suspect materials checked by a qualified contractor or an IRSST-recognized lab and never to do asbestos work themselves. Quebec treats material as asbestos-containing from 0.1% asbestos, a stricter line than most provinces.

faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

Of Laval's 101,460 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 17% were built before 1961 and 67% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).

Don't dry-sand, use a heat gun or power-wash it. Contain the work area, mist surfaces, clean with a HEPA vacuum, and keep children and pregnant people away until cleanup is done. No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. and Yukon must include lead in pre-renovation or demolition hazard inspections.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Laval: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Laval: ASHRAE levels, 1 reporting rule that apply, and 4 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Laval: 1 mandatory reporting rule and 4 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Laval
sections.html:
• No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.QC).
  • Règlement sur la déclaration obligatoire de la performance environnementale de certains bâtiments (Loi sur la performance environnementale des bâtiments, chapitre P-9.02) (in force - first declarations due June 30, 2027): From Jan 1, 2027: buildings of 5,000 m2+ (not exclusively residential), residential or partly residential buildings with 50+ units, and buildings owned by public bodies other than municipal bodies (buildings under 100 m2 excepted, subject to a metering condition in the text). From Jan 1, 2028: buildings of 2,000 m2+ (not exclusively residential) and residential buildings with 25+ units. Source

• Efficient Solutions Program - Energy Analysis component (Hydro-Québec): Pays for eligible costs of an energy analysis (including in-house labour): 40% of eligible costs when the report is accepted and 60% after at least one measure is implemented (up to 100% in total). Caps for energy-efficiency analyses: existing buildings with 1-2 GWh reference use, $8,000 + $12,000 ($20,000 total), analysis must identify at least 100,000 kWh/yr of savings; over 2 GWh, $20,000 + $30,000 ($50,000 total), at least 200,000 kWh/yr. Analyses that also cover demand-response measures: up to $60,000 ($24,000 + $36,000 for buildings over 2 GWh). Details
  • ÉcoPerformance - Analyse de mesures de réduction des GES (Gouvernement du Québec (MELCCFP)): Standard analysis (energy study, fuel-switching study, fugitive-emissions study): 50% of eligible expenses, max $25,000 per site for small/medium energy users (under 36,000 GJ/yr non-electric) or $75,000 for large users. Complex analysis: 75%, max $100,000 / $300,000. Paid 50% on the signed purchase order and the rest after the engineer-signed report is accepted; project must finish within 24 months. Details
  • Energy audit and implementation - Feasibility Study grant (Énergir): 50% of the pre-tax cost of a feasibility study, max $50,000. Follow-on implementation grant: $1 per m3 of natural gas saved in the first year (max $1,000,000 per account), plus up to $15,000 for energy tracking. Details
  • Recommissioning of mechanical systems grant (Énergir): Investigation phase: 75% of eligible costs; implementation: $1 per m3 of gas saved up to 75% of eligible costs (measures with payback over 1 year); transfer and continuous-monitoring phases: 75% of eligible costs. Up to $100,000 per project in total. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Laval buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: Yes, above certain sizes: Règlement sur la déclaration obligatoire de la performance environnementale de certains bâtiments (Loi sur la performance environnementale des bâtiments, chapitre P-9.02).

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Laval?
faq.a: Yes: Efficient Solutions Program - Energy Analysis component; ÉcoPerformance - Analyse de mesures de réduction des GES; Energy audit and implementation - Feasibility Study grant; Recommissioning of mechanical systems grant. Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
